what_its_for: Infliximab is used to treat conditions where your immune system attacks your own body. It helps reduce swelling, pain, and damage caused by diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes inflammation.
how_to_take: Infliximab is given as an IV infusion (a drip into your vein) by a doctor or nurse in a clinic or infusion center. You cannot give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion usually takes about 2 hours. You will be watched by medical staff during and after your infusion for any reactions. Do not miss your scheduled appointments.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your weight and the condition being treated. Most people start with doses at Week 0, Week 2, and Week 6, then receive maintenance doses every 4 to 8 weeks after that. Your doctor may adjust your dose if needed. Always follow your doctor's exact schedule.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule your infusion appointment, call your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible. Do not try to catch up on your own. Your doctor will tell you when to come in for your next dose. Staying on schedule is very important for this medicine to work properly.
storage: Infliximab is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals. You do not need to store it at home. The medicine must be kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and protected from light. It should never be frozen. Once mixed for your infusion, it must be used within a certain time period by the healthcare team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine lowers your immune system's ability to fight germs. Do not receive live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, or nasal flu spray) while using infliximab without talking to your doctor first. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as your risk of skin cancer may be slightly higher. Limit alcohol and talk to your doctor before starting any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: fever, chills, or signs of infection; chest pain or difficulty breathing; rash, hives, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat during or after your infusion; unusual tiredness or weakness; numbness or tingling; vision changes; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain; or if you notice any new or worsening symptoms. Also tell your doctor if you have been exposed to tuberculosis (TB) or if you have ever had hepatitis B.
when_it_works: Some people start to feel better within a few weeks, but it may take 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefit of infliximab. Do not stop treatment just because you are feeling better. Continuing your scheduled infusions helps keep your condition under control. Talk to your doctor if you feel your symptoms are not improving.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women should talk to their doctor before using infliximab. Babies born to mothers who used infliximab during pregnancy should not receive live vaccines for at least 6 months after birth. Elderly patients and children may use infliximab under close medical supervision. People with a history of infections, cancer, heart failure, or nervous system problems should let their doctor know before starting treatment, as extra monitoring may be needed.
